steps.title: Obtain Tudor domain constructs
steps.instruction: Acquire the following plasmids: SMN Tudor domain (residues 82‑147) in pET24d with N‑terminal His‑GST tag and TEV site (gift from M. Sattler); NusG Tudor (123‑181) in pET28b(+) with N‑terminal His‑SUMO tag (available from Burmann Lab); RfaH Tudor (101‑162) in pET28b(+) with N‑terminal His‑SUMO tag (GenScript, also available from Burmann Lab). Verify each construct by DNA sequencing.

steps.title: Transform constructs into competent cells
steps.instruction: Thaw chemically competent E. coli BL21 Star™ (λDE3) on ice for ~30 min. Warm LB‑Kanamycin agar plates at 37 °C. Pipette 1–2 µL plasmid (~50 ng/µL) into 25–50 µL competent cells, mix gently, incubate on ice 20–30 min, heat‑shock at 42 °C for 45 s, return to ice 2 min, add 400 µL LB, shake at 37 °C for 1 h, centrifuge 3400 ×g 2 min, discard supernatant, streak cells onto the LB‑Kan plates, incubate 16–20 h at 37 °C, seal plates with parafilm and store at 4 °C (up to 2 weeks, preferably <1 week). Maintain sterility (70 % EtOH, flame/laminar flow).

steps.title: Express uniformly 15N‑labelled proteins
steps.instruction: Inoculate a single colony into 5 mL LB + 50 µg/mL Kanamycin, grow 37 °C, 200 rpm for 6–8 h. Transfer 1 mL of this preculture into 50 mL M9 medium in a 250 mL flask, grow 37 °C, 200 rpm for 16–20 h. Scale up to 1 L M9 in a 5 L flask, grow 37 °C, 200 rpm, monitor OD₆₀₀ to 0.6–0.8. Add IPTG: 0.5 mM for RfaH Tudor, 1 mM for SMN and NusG. Incubate 25 °C, 200 rpm for 16–20 h (NusG & RfaH) or 4 h (SMN). Harvest cells 4000 ×g 20 min at 4 °C, discard supernatant, keep pellets at –80 °C (up to 1–2 months). Thaw pellets at 20–22 °C, keep on ice.

steps.title: Purify proteins to NMR quality
steps.instruction: Add to lysis buffer (50 mL per 10 g wet pellet): one Roche cOmplete EDTA‑free protease inhibitor tablet, 5 µL HL‑SAN DNase I, 10 mM MgSO₄. Resuspend pellets, homogenize with Emulsiflex C3 at 4 °C (≥3 passes). Centrifuge 19000 ×g 45 min at 4 °C, collect supernatant. Load onto a manually packed Ni²⁺‑NTA (HisPur™) column equilibrated with lysis buffer at 20–22 °C (load twice). Wash 10 CV lysis buffer, then wash with lysis buffer + 25 mM imidazole. Elute with 5 CV elution buffer, keep fractions on ice. Verify by SDS‑PAGE. Add His‑tagged SenP1 (Sumo protease) or TEV protease, dialyze 16–20 h for tag cleavage. Check cleavage by SDS‑PAGE; if incomplete, add more protease, incubate RT 2–3 h. Perform a second Ni‑NTA run to bind uncleaved protein, collect flow‑through (target protein). Combine target fractions, concentrate to 1–2 mL with Vivaspin 15R (3 kDa MWCO) at 4 °C. Equilibrate a HiLoad 16/600 Superdex75 column with size‑exclusion buffer on an ÄKTA FPLC at 4 °C, inject concentrated sample, monitor UV, collect protein peaks, confirm purity by SDS‑PAGE. Pool protein‑containing fractions, exchange into final NMR buffer using Vivaspin 15R (3 kDa MWCO). Flash‑freeze aliquots in liquid N₂, store at –80 °C; thaw at 20–22 °C before use. Keep all buffers cold, use fresh Ni‑NTA resin each purification, avoid air bubbles in the SEC column, and verify A₂₆₀/A₂₈₀ ratio of 0.5–0.6 (nanodrop or UV‑Vis).

steps.title: Measure heteronuclear NOE (hetNOE)
steps.instruction: For each magnetic field (B₁ e.g., 11.7 T, ¹H = 500 MHz; B₂ e.g., 21.1 T, ¹H = 900 MHz) perform the 2D ¹⁵N{¹H}‑NOE experiment (pulse sequence hsqcnoef3gpsi). Set sample temperature appropriate for stability, insert sample, lock/tune/match/shim. Calibrate ¹H 90° pulse, water carrier, ¹⁵N 90° pulse. Set ¹⁵N carrier 116–122 ppm (use 119 ppm if unknown) and sweep width 36 ppm; optionally calibrate ¹³C (119 ppm carrier, 110 ppm for CSA decoupling). Set ¹H and ¹⁵N sweep widths, acquire 2048 × 256 complex points, number of scans (ns) = 8 for ~500 µM sample (adjust for lower concentration), recycling delay d₁ ≥ 3 s, check receiver gain (rga), start acquisition (zg). Ensure phase‑cycling ns is a multiple of 4, 8 or 16. After acquisition, split interleaved data (split, rows = 2). Process Reference and Saturated spectra with identical parameters; record intensity scaling factor (nc_proc) and apply to both. Convert Bruker files to .ucsf (bruk2ucsf), open in NMRFAM‑SPARKY, import BMRB assignments, save project. Generate peak lists with data‑height column (lt → Options → Data height). Record noise (st command). In relaxGUI, create a new Steady‑state NOE analysis, load N and H spins (PDB or sequence), add Reference and Saturated peak‑list files with IDs, set Baseplane RMSD for error, assign spectrum types, execute. Rename output noe.700.out to .txt, import to Excel, compute per‑residue hetNOE, plot vs residue, calculate median and standard deviation for the average hetNOE. Repeat the entire acquisition and analysis at the second field.

steps.title: Determine longitudinal relaxation rates (R1)
steps.instruction: For each field (B₁ and B₂) record inversion‑recovery experiments (pulse sequence hsqct1etf3gpsi) at relaxation delays d₇ = 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6, 2.0, 2.4 s. Follow the same setup steps as in hetNOE (temperature, lock, calibrations, sweep widths, 2048 × 256 points, ns as appropriate, d₁ ≥ 3 s, zg). After acquisition, process the 0.4 s spectrum first, note its intensity scaling factor (nc_proc), then process all other delay spectra using the same scaling factor. Convert all processed files to .ucsf, open in SPARKY, generate peak lists with data‑height, save. In relaxGUI start a new R1 analysis, load N and H spins, add the seven peak‑list files with corresponding IDs, set Baseplane RMSD = 10 (to avoid crashes), assign each ID its relaxation time, choose Exponential model I(t)=I∞ − I₀ e^(−Rₓ t). Execute. Rename r1.700.out to .txt, import to Excel, obtain per‑residue R₁ values, plot, compute median and SD for average R₁. Estimate uncertainties by bootstrapping: repeat analysis at least three times, each time omitting two of the seven peak lists (use five). Calculate SD of the four datasets (original + three bootstraps) for each residue. Repeat the whole procedure at the second magnetic field.

steps.title: Determine transverse relaxation rates (R1ρ and R2)
steps.instruction: For each field (B₁ and B₂) acquire T₁ρ experiments (pulse sequence hsqctretf3gpsi) with spin‑lock delays d₃₁ = 0, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65 ms. Use the same spectrometer setup as before (temperature, calibrations, sweep widths, 2048 × 256 points, ns, d₁ ≥ 3 s, zg). Process the 0 ms dataset first, record its scaling factor, then process the remaining datasets with the same factor. Convert to .ucsf, open in SPARKY, generate peak lists with data‑height, save. In relaxGUI start a new R2 analysis (actually R₁ρ), load spins, add the seven peak‑list files with IDs, assign relaxation times 0, 0.015, 0.025, 0.035, 0.045, 0.055, 0.065 s, choose two‑parameter exponential model I(t)=I₀ e^(−Rₓ t), execute. Rename r2.700.out to .txt, import to Excel, obtain per‑residue R₁ρ values. Compute R₂ for each residue using R₁ρ = R₁ cos²θ + R₂ sin²θ, where θ = arctan(ν₁/Δν) and Δν is the offset of the rf field (as defined in Massi et al., 2004). Calculate median and SD for average R₁ρ and R₂, propagate errors from R₁ and R₁ρ. Repeat at the second magnetic field.

steps.title: Compute theoretical rates with HYDRONMR
steps.instruction: Create a working directory, copy the protein PDB file into it. Write an input file hydronmr.dat containing: molecule name, output file name, PDB filename, AER = 3.3 Å, temperature = 298 K, magnetic fields (e.g., 16.4 T and 18.8 T), N‑H bond length = 1.02 Å, CSA = ‑173 ppm. Leave NSIG, SIGMIN, SIGMAX, ETA, IFLAG, gyromagnetic ratio, and number‑of‑fields unchanged. Run HYDRONMR; the program writes a .res file in the same folder. Open the .res file with a text editor, extract the per‑residue theoretical R₁, R₂, and diffusion parameters, and plot versus residue number in Excel or GraphPad Prism. Note that the .res file also provides translational diffusion coefficient, rotational diffusion coefficient, rotational diffusion anisotropy, and mean rotational correlation time.

steps.title: Calculate rotational correlation time τc
steps.instruction: Open a spreadsheet, import per‑residue R₁ and R₂ values (and their uncertainties) from Steps 2 and 3. Compute T₁ = 1/R₁ and T₂ = 1/R₂. Use the empirical equation τ_c ≈ (14 π ν_N) / (6 T₁ T₂ − 7), where ν_N is the ¹⁵N Larmor frequency (Hz) for the field used. Calculate τ_c for each residue, then obtain the median and standard deviation as the average τ_c and its spread. Propagate errors from R₁ and R₂ to τ_c. Repeat the calculation for the data obtained at the second magnetic field. (Tensor2 can also provide τ_c as an alternative.)

steps.title: Determine diffusion tensor with Tensor2
steps.instruction: Create a new folder, launch the Tensor2 program (tensor2). In the GUI: File → Open data file and load a file containing the experimental R₁, R₂, and hetNOE values with their uncertainties. File → Open PDB file and load the protein structure. Visualization → Definition to select residues for analysis. Setup → Spectro to enter the spectrometer frequency (Hz). Optionally choose Isotropy → Fit to obtain τ_c. Then select Anisotropy → Fit to compute the diffusion tensor (axially symmetric D∥/D⊥ or fully anisotropic D_xx, D_yy, D_zz). Set Nb Cycle = 500 and click Start Monte‑Carlo to estimate uncertainties. Results are written to text files resaniso.0 (isotropic fit) and resaniso.1 (anisotropic fit).

steps.title: Perform model‑free analysis
steps.instruction: Open relaxGUI, start a new Model‑free analysis (File → New analysis → Model‑free analysis). Define the results directory. Load the spin system for backbone ¹⁵N and ¹H (Spin editor → load from PDB or sequence). Add relaxation data sets: hetNOE, R₁, and R₂ from both magnetic fields (Add → specify ID, type, frequency, file, free‑format). Load metadata (temperature control, calibration; select “no control” if absent). In the main window click Dipole‑dipole, confirm average N‑H distance 1.02 Å. Set Chemical Shift Anisotropy to –172 ppm. Confirm isotopes (¹⁵N, ¹H). Keep default settings for local τ_m, model grid, Monte‑Carlo simulations, maximum interactions, and protocol mode. Click Execute to run the analysis. Output folders for each model contain files S².out, R_ex.out, τ_e.out (rename .out to .txt). Import these into Excel or GraphPad Prism to view per‑residue order parameters (S²), exchange contributions (R_ex), and effective internal correlation times (τ_e). Alternative programs: FAST Modelfree or Tensor2 (single‑field only).

description: Proteins are intrinsically dynamic biomolecules. Although a determination of protein structures provides an excellent ab-initio information about the structural arrangements of proteins and thereby provides also insight into its function, it predominantly represents merely the time-averaged conformation out of several dynamic conformations adopted by the protein molecule critical for its functionality (Schiro et al., 2020). Therefore, a comprehensive depiction of biomolecular dynamics in solution is of high importance not only to complement the structural information but also for the thorough understanding of the biomolecular functional spectrum (Sekhar and Kay, 2019). The protein molecule undergoes a variety of structural transitions at timescales such as the fast (ps–ns) as well as the slow (μs–s) timescale displaying physical motions ranging from bond vibrations, loop motions as well as backbone torsion angle and side-chain rotations with implications in enzyme catalysis, conformational changes, ligand binding and protein folding/unfolding etc. (Figure 1) (Kovermann et al., 2016; Marsh and Teichmann, 2015). Probing protein dynamics involves the systematic characterization of these embedded complex motions occurring at various timescales governed by the conformations accompanied by distinct energy barriers (Kovermann et al., 2016; Markwick et al., 2008). Solution NMR spectroscopy is one of the most powerful as well as most versatile techniques commonly used for the structural and dynamical characterization of biomolecules. The 15N NMR relaxation experiments for the characterization of protein backbone dynamics are based on the 2D [15N,1H] heteronuclear single quantum coherence (HSQC) experiment which provides information about all 15N atoms bound to 1H atoms (Bodenhausen and Ruben, 1980).
